visuals.title: The life of a variable: ordinary local vs static local

stages.name: 1. The function is called
stages.detail: A new frame appears on the call stack.

stages.name: 2. The variable is created
stages.detail: An ordinary local is created every call. A static local is created only on the FIRST call, in static memory.

stages.name: 3. The function runs
stages.detail: Both are used the same way inside the function. Only code inside the function can see them.

stages.name: 4. The function returns
stages.detail: The ordinary local is destroyed and loses its value. The static local stays alive and keeps its value.

stages.name: 5. The next call
stages.detail: The ordinary local starts fresh again. The static local still has its old value and its initial value is not set a second time.

visuals.title: Match each term to its meaning

pairs.meaning: Declared inside a function or block, usable only there
Declared outside all functions, visible everywhere below it
The part of the program where a name can be used
How long the variable's box exists in memory
An inner variable with the same name hides the outer one
Created once, keeps its value between calls, visible only in its function

goal: After this you can say where a variable can be used (scope) and how long it lives (lifetime), explain why globals are risky, and use a static local variable to remember a value between function calls.
warmup: Think of a hostel. A notice stuck inside your room is read only by people in your room: that is a local variable. A notice on the main gate is read by everybody: that is a global variable, and everybody can also scribble on it, so it gets messy. Now think of a canteen token counter. The cashier does not restart from 1 for every customer. The counter remembers the last number. A static variable gives a function that kind of memory.
definition: Scope is the part of the program where a variable name can be used. A local variable is declared inside a function or inside a { } block. It can be used only there (block scope). A global variable is declared outside all functions and can be used by every function below it. Lifetime is how long the variable's box exists. An ordinary local variable is created each time the block runs and destroyed when it ends. A static local variable is created and set up only once, and keeps its value for the whole program, although only its own function can see it.
howItWorks: Open the scope trace and look at the call stack panel. The global total sits in its own area outside every function. When the { } block starts, a new x appears and hides the outer x. When the block ends, it disappears. Inside main, a local total hides the global total, but the function show() has no total of its own, so it uses the global one. This is called shadowing: the nearest declaration wins. Now open the counter trace. The ordinary variable normal is created again from 0 on every call, so it is always 1. The static variable calls is created once. The line static int calls = 0; runs only the first time. On later calls it is skipped and calls keeps counting. Why avoid globals? Any function can change them, so when a value is wrong you do not know who changed it. It is also hard to reuse a function that depends on a global. Prefer local variables and pass values with parameters and return.

worked.problem: Show scope and shadowing: a global total, a local x inside a { } block that hides another x, and a local total in main that hides the global one. Print each value and show that the function show() still sees the global.
pseudocode: OPEN block: new x = 50, PRINT x
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[Global total = 100]
  B --> C[x = 5]
  C --> D[Block: new x = 50]
  D --> E[/Print inner x/]
  E --> F[Block ends]
  F --> G[/Print outer x/]
  G --> H[Local total = 1]
  H --> I[/Print main total/]
  I --> J[Call show]
  J --> K[/Print global total/]
  K --> L([End])

sample.title: Global, local and block scope
sample.expectedOutput:
inner x = 50
outer x = 5
main total = 1
show sees total = 100

explanation.text: A global variable: declared outside every function.
show has no total of its own, so this is the global total.
Local to main.
A new x with block scope. It hides the outer x until the closing brace.
Uses the nearest x, the inner one: 50.
The block is over, so x is the outer one again: 5.
A local total in main. It shadows the global total, which is still 100.
show() cannot see main's local total, so it prints the global 100.

steps.note: The global total (100) already exists before main starts. It is created outside every function.
main creates its local x = 5.
The { } block opens and makes a NEW x = 50. It hides (shadows) the outer x while we are inside the block.
Inside the block, x means the inner x: 50.
The block ends. The inner x dies. The outer x was never changed.
Back to the outer x: 5.
main declares its own local total = 1. In main this name now hides the global total. The global one is still 100.
Inside main, total means the local one: 1.
main calls show(). show has no total of its own, so it uses the global one.
show prints the global total: 100. A local variable of main is not visible inside show.
return 0 ends the program.

  B --> C[static last grows 101, 102, 103]
  C --> D[2 calls to plainToken]
  D --> E[last restarts at 100 each time: 101, 101]

sample.title: Token numbers: static vs ordinary

explanation.text: static: set to 100 only on the first call.
Adds 1 to the remembered value.
Returns it. The static variable keeps the new value for the next call.
Ordinary local: becomes 100 again on every call.
First token: 101.
Second token: 102, because last remembered 101.
Third token: 103.
plainToken gives 101.
plainToken gives 101 again: it forgot.

variations.when: Inside a function. It is created at each call and dies on return. Use it for almost everything.
Declared inside { } such as a loop body or an if block. It dies at the closing brace.
variations.example: if (x > 0) { int y = x * 2; }  // y is gone after }

variations.when: Declared outside all functions. Seen by every function below it. Avoid it except for fixed constants.
A function must remember a value between calls (counters, token numbers).
An inner variable with the same name hides the outer one. It works but confuses readers. Prefer different names.

mistakes.error: error: 'x' was not declared in this scope
error: 'c' was not declared in this scope
No compiler error. hit() always prints 1 because an ordinary local starts from 0 on every call. Use static when the value must be remembered.
No compiler error. The declaration creates a new local total that hides the global one, so the global never changes. Remove the type word to use the global.

examTips: Local = only inside its function or { } block. Global = outside all functions. Say 'scope' for where, 'lifetime' for how long.
static local: created and initialised ONCE, keeps its value between calls, still visible only inside its function.
In output questions, mark which variable is ordinary (restarts every call) and which is static (keeps counting).
When two variables have the same name, the one in the nearest enclosing block wins (shadowing).
Reason to avoid globals: any function can change them, so bugs are hard to find. Use parameters and return values instead.
romanSummary: Local variable sirf apne function ya { } block ke andar chalta hai. Global variable sab functions mein nazar aata hai.
Scope ka matlab hai variable kahan use ho sakta hai, aur lifetime ka matlab hai wo kitni der memory mein rehta hai.
Normal local variable har call par naya banta hai aur return par khatam ho jata hai.
static local variable sirf ek dafa banta hai aur calls ke darmiyan apni value yaad rakhta hai, jaise counter.
Globals kam se kam use karein, kyunke koi bhi function unhein badal sakta hai aur bug dhoondna mushkil ho jata hai.

practice.hint: Local means private to its function.
practice.explanation: A local variable is visible only in the function or block where it is declared.
n is created once and keeps growing: 1, 2, 3.

practice.explanation: Declare result before the if so that it lives long enough to be printed.

practice.prompt: Write a function int nextId() that returns 1 the first time, 2 the second time, and so on, using a static variable. In main call it three times and print the three numbers on one line separated by spaces.

practice.explanation: The static id remembers its value, so the three calls give 1, 2, 3.

quiz.prompt: What is the main property of a static local variable?
options: It keeps its value between function calls
It is visible in every function
It is created on every call
quiz.answer: It keeps its value between function calls
quiz.explanation: A static local is created once and keeps its value for the whole program.

quiz.prompt: Where is a global variable declared?
quiz.hint: Look at where total = 100 is written.
quiz.explanation: Globals are declared outside every function.

quiz.prompt: What happens to an ordinary local variable when its function returns?
quiz.explanation: Ordinary locals live only while the function runs.

quiz.prompt: Why should we avoid global variables?
options: Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to find
quiz.answer: Any function can change them, so bugs are hard to find
quiz.hint: Think about who can modify them.
quiz.explanation: Shared changeable data makes it hard to see which function caused a wrong value.

quiz.prompt: int x = 5; { int x = 9; } cout << x;  What is printed?
quiz.hint: The inner x dies at the closing brace.
quiz.explanation: The inner x belongs to the block only. After the block the outer x (5) is used.
